title: Deep-space soft-decision decoding inside the DRAM sense amp
idea: Adapted from deep-space telemetry (Voyager/Mars links decode near the noise floor with soft-decision LDPC): each sense amp reports the bit plus a 2-bit confidence derived from its latch time-to-decision (measured by a shared counter), and an on-die LDPC decoder over 512-bit codewords uses those soft values. Ambiguous bits from half-charge cells are flagged and corrected rather than guessed.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): reading ~2-2.5 fF cells instead of 4.5-5.4 fF lets capacitor aspect ratio drop from 60-75:1 toward ~35:1, cutting etch/deposition cost; soft decoding buys ~2-3 dB effective margin over hard SECDED.

title: NAND-style read-reference tracking keyed to time since refresh
idea: Adapted from NAND flash controllers that shift read thresholds as charge drifts: each mat holds a few dummy cells rewritten at every refresh; at read time a small comparator samples their decayed voltage and shifts the sense-amp reference so the decision threshold follows the leakage curve instead of sitting at a fixed VARY/2.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): a moving reference recovers ~30-40% of signal margin late in the refresh window, allowing 2-4x longer tREFI and cutting refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit) and bandwidth loss proportionally.

title: Bridge strain-gauge sentinels: deliberately weak canary cells gate refresh
idea: Adapted from structural health monitoring, where cheap gauges alarm before the bridge fails: each subarray includes a column of sentinel cells built with ~70% of nominal capacitor height (one extra trim step) so they leak first; a subarray is refreshed only when its sentinels begin to flip, checked for free during normal activations.
why: Refresh power (fact 3): most subarrays retain far longer than the 32/64 ms worst case; sentinel-gated refresh can cut refresh operations 3-6x at typical temperatures, with a margin tied to real local leakage and temperature.

title: SYN-cookie style epoch-keyed row scrambling against hammering
idea: Adapted from network security's stateless key rotation (SYN cookies, ASLR re-randomization): the DRAM die applies a keyed bijective permutation (a 4-round Feistel on row-address bits) between logical and physical rows inside each subarray and re-keys every epoch by migrating rows during refresh slots, so no attacker holds a fixed set of physical neighbors for more than one epoch.
why: Row hammer at ~1k activations (fact 9): turns deterministic double-sided attacks into random spraying, raising the effective per-victim threshold by roughly rows-per-subarray/2 without per-row counters, saving counter area and PRAC timing penalties.

title: Seismic base-isolation shield lines buried between wordlines
idea: Adapted from base-isolated buildings that decouple a structure from ground shaking: insert a grounded buried shield line (a dummy recessed gate held at slight negative bias) between every pair of active buried wordlines, so aggressor wordline swings and hot electrons injected into the substrate are absorbed by the shield rather than the victim storage node.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): blocks both electrostatic coupling and trap-assisted charge pumping, potentially raising flip thresholds 10x+ at ~15-25% array-area cost (6F2 to ~7.5F2), trading density for deleting counters, RFM and victim-refresh overhead.

title: Psychoacoustic masking applied to bit-plane refresh of AI tensors
idea: Adapted from MP3/AAC perceptual coding, which spends bits only where the ear notices: the controller stores bf16/fp8 weights bit-plane transposed so sign, exponent and high-mantissa planes sit in normally refreshed rows while low-mantissa planes sit in rows refreshed 8-16x less often; a per-layer sensitivity score (Hessian trace computed at load) sets how many planes each tensor sends to the slow-refresh zone.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3): 40-60% of weight bits tolerate BER ~1e-4 with <0.1% accuracy loss, roughly halving refresh power for weight memory and letting those planes live in weaker, cheaper cells.

title: CDMA code-division storage across simultaneously activated rows
idea: Adapted from CDMA cellular radio, where users share a channel through orthogonal spreading codes and despreading averages out noise: k data bits are stored across N cells on one bitline with Walsh-coded charge levels written by N simultaneously activated wordlines; on read the same multi-row activation sums charge on the bitline and a code-matched sense sequence recovers each bit with processing gain, so any single leaky or dead cell only adds noise.
why: Capacitor wall and retention tail (facts 1, 3): processing gain of ~10log(N/k) dB lets individual cells shrink to ~1-2 fF and makes isolated leaky cells irrelevant, removing most row/column repair and relaxing refresh.

title: Hybrid-ARQ incremental-redundancy ECC with far-stored heavy parity
idea: Adapted from LTE/5G hybrid ARQ, where the first transmission carries a light code and extra parity is sent only if decoding fails: each 64 B line carries only a small inline detect-and-correct-one code, while a strong Reed-Solomon parity per 4 KB region lives in a separate low-traffic row group and is fetched only on the rare detected failure.
why: ECC overhead and data movement (facts 5, 8): common-case reads move ~1.5% overhead instead of 12.5% while still tolerating raw BER ~1e-5 from weaker cells, reclaiming ~10% bandwidth and ~8% capacity.

title: Camera hot-pixel map: cell-level defect substitution table on die
idea: Adapted from CMOS image sensors, which ship with hundreds of dead pixels mapped out and patched in the ISP instead of scrapping the sensor: retention-weak and stuck cells found at test or in the field are recorded as compressed (row, column) entries in a small table on the logic base die, and a substitution engine overwrites those exact bit positions on every read with bits held in the table's own SRAM.
why: Yield and repair cost (facts 3, 7): per-cell substitution handles a 1e-6 weak-cell density at ~0.3% area instead of ~3-5% row/column redundancy, and lets fabs relax capacitor targets because the worst 1-ppm tail is handled individually.

title: Display mura compensation for sense-amp offset to shrink periphery
idea: Adapted from OLED/LCD panels, which measure per-region non-uniformity at the factory and apply stored correction constants at runtime: each sense amp's offset is measured at test or boot and stored as a 3-bit trim in a dense one-time-programmable array, which injects a small compensating charge before sensing so sense-amp transistors can be drawn at minimum size.
why: Periphery at ~49% of die (fact 7): sense amps oversized for mismatch are a big periphery block; offset trimming could shrink them ~30-40%, cutting die area ~5-8% while keeping read margin for weaker cells.

title: SerDes decision-feedback equalization across neighboring bitlines
idea: Adapted from high-speed SerDes receivers, which subtract known inter-symbol interference using already-decided bits: even-column sense amps resolve first, and their decided values drive a small coupling-cancel capacitor onto the adjacent odd bitlines before those resolve, removing the data-dependent bitline-to-bitline coupling that eats margin.
why: Charge wall and pattern-dependent failures (facts 1, 8): bitline coupling consumes ~15-25% of sense margin at tight pitch; cancelling it restores margin worth ~1 fF of storage capacitance and removes worst-case data-pattern errors.

title: Power-electronics snubber: slew-shaped wordline edges cut hammer disturbance
idea: Adapted from snubbers and slew-rate control that suppress ringing and EMI in power converters: wordline drivers use a programmable current-starved two-segment edge (fast to ~70%, then slow ramp, and a slow falling tail), reducing dV/dt coupling and the abrupt trap-assisted electron emission at wordline fall that drives row hammer and RowPress flips.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): disturbance scales with edge rate and injection at wordline fall; shaped edges may raise flip thresholds 2-4x at a ~1-2 ns tRAS/tRP cost, shrinking mitigation-refresh overhead.

title: TCP congestion control for refresh: AIMD on correctable-error signals
idea: Adapted from TCP's additive-increase/multiplicative-decrease loop, which probes for capacity until packets drop: each bank's refresh interval is lengthened in small steps while on-die ECC reports zero corrections and halved immediately when the correction rate crosses a threshold, so refresh tracks the bank's real retention at its current temperature and age.
why: Refresh cost (fact 3): typical banks retain 4-10x longer than worst-case spec; a closed loop riding the ECC margin could cut refresh energy and bandwidth loss 50-80%, with ECC as the safety net against variable-retention cells.

title: SSD over-provisioning: hidden spare rows with a live remap engine
idea: Adapted from SSD flash translation layers that hide 7-28% spare blocks and remap failing ones in the field: each bank reserves ~2% spare rows invisible to the host, and a small CAM in the row-decoder path redirects any row that accumulates ECC corrections to a spare, copying its data in the background during refresh slots.
why: Field reliability and test cost (facts 3, 9): moves repair from a one-time factory fuse step to lifelong adaptive repair, allowing shorter factory retention screens and absorbing aging-induced weak rows; raises effective yield several percent.

title: Self-clearing film-capacitor electrodes for thin high-k DRAM capacitors
idea: Adapted from metallized polymer film capacitors, whose ultra-thin electrode vaporizes around a breakdown spot so the part survives with negligibly less area: use a 2-3 nm top electrode of a low-melting conductive oxide so a local dielectric breakdown burns a sub-10-nm hole in the electrode, isolating the defect instead of shorting the cell.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): dielectric thickness is set by breakdown and leakage tails; tolerating pinholes could allow ~20-30% thinner high-k and proportionally higher Cs or lower aspect ratio without yield loss to shorted cells.

title: pH-buffer storage node: antiferroelectric plateau resists leakage droop
idea: Adapted from chemical buffer solutions, which hold pH nearly constant by drawing on a reservoir as acid is added: add an antiferroelectric layer (Zr-rich HfZrO tuned so its field-induced transition sits just below VARY) in the storage capacitor, so leakage first drains the stored polarization reservoir while node voltage stays flat near the plateau, delaying the fall below the sense threshold.
why: Retention tail and charge wall (facts 1, 3): an effective Q-V plateau could give 3-5x more charge per volt near the operating point, extending retention 3-5x or allowing a much shorter capacitor.

title: Railway sidings: on-die hot-row SRAM cache absorbs hammering
idea: Adapted from rail yards that pull a heavily used train onto a siding to keep the main line clear: each bank has a 16-entry row-wide SRAM siding; when a row's approximate activation count (Misra-Gries tracker) crosses ~200, the row is copied into the siding and served from SRAM until it cools, so the physical row stops toggling.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) and activation energy (fact 8): the aggressor physically stops activating, eliminating victim-refresh storms and saving ~1 nJ per avoided activation on hot rows, for ~1% die area.

title: Solar bypass diodes: segment switches replace column redundancy
idea: Adapted from photovoltaic panels, whose bypass diodes route current around a shaded or failed string instead of losing the panel: each bitline is split into 4 segments joined by small pass switches; a segment with a defect (short, leaky cluster) is opened and its cells skipped via a decoder offset, so only a quarter-column is lost instead of swapping in a full redundant column.
why: Periphery and repair area (fact 7): spare columns plus fuses and muxes cost several percent of area; segment bypass trades ~1-2% switch overhead for removing most column redundancy and lets arrays ship with more local defects.

title: Building expansion joints: compliant spring microbumps for HBM stacks
idea: Adapted from expansion joints that let bridges and buildings move with temperature without cracking: replace rigid microbumps in HBM stacks with helical or serpentine copper micro-springs electroplated in a sacrificial resist mold, absorbing CTE mismatch and warpage during bonding and thermal cycling so TSVs and bumps do not crack.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): much of the 20-30% stack yield loss and early-life failure comes from bonding stress and warpage; compliant joints could recover ~5-10 points of stack yield and allow thinner dies.

title: CD-ROM cross-interleaving to retire row and column redundancy
idea: Adapted from the CD's cross-interleaved Reed-Solomon code, which spreads each codeword along the disc so a scratch becomes many small correctable errors: each ECC codeword's symbols are mapped diagonally across 8 subarrays, 8 sub-wordline drivers and 8 local sense-amp stripes, so losing any one driver, stripe or column produces at most one symbol error per codeword.
why: Repair area and burst failures (fact 7): periphery defects that now need redundant drivers and fuses become routine single-symbol corrections, freeing ~2-4% die area and raising yield on large 32-64 Gb dies.

title: Antivirus signature updates for fleet-learned hammer patterns
idea: Adapted from antivirus engines and immune memory, where a threat seen once anywhere becomes a signature everywhere: hyperscalers stream correctable-error locations and controller activation histograms to a central service that learns new hammer shapes (many-sided, half-double), compiles them into small finite-state detectors and pushes them fleet-wide as memory-controller microcode updates.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): mitigations frozen in silicon are bypassed within a year; patchable detection lets vendors ship lighter in-DRAM mitigation and keeps cheaper, more hammer-prone dies usable.

title: Election risk-limiting audits replace exhaustive retention testing
idea: Adapted from risk-limiting election audits that certify a result by sampling ballots until statistical confidence is reached: wafer retention test samples random rows per mat with a sequential probability ratio test, stops early on clearly good mats, and escalates to a full retention sweep only for mats whose samples look risky; residual uncertainty is covered by in-field ECC.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): long retention and pattern tests tie up expensive testers for minutes per die; sequential sampling could cut test time 3-5x, freeing tester capital and raising throughput.

title: Grid fault-current limiters islanding shorted wordlines per mat
idea: Adapted from power grids that use fault-current limiters and islanding so one short does not black out a region: each mat's local wordline-driver supply has a self-tripping current limiter (a small overcurrent-sensing latch), so a WL-to-BL or WL-to-plate short isolates its own mat instead of collapsing VPP for the whole bank; the mat is then marked out and its addresses remapped.
why: Yield (facts 4, 7): hard shorts are among the few defects that kill whole banks or dies; islanding turns a die-killer into ~0.1% capacity loss, raising yield on large-die parts by several percent.

title: SSD-controller playbook: 28nm CXL controller with page-level LDPC
idea: Adapted from NAND flash, which became cheap by pairing weak cells with smart controllers: a 28 nm CXL memory controller built in existing mature logic fabs applies 4 KB-codeword LDPC, with an on-chip SRAM write-combining buffer for read-modify-write, to unmodified commodity or lower-grade DRAM, exposing a byte-addressable device that tolerates raw BER ~1e-4.
why: Supply and cost per bit (facts 3, 4): operators can buy dies that fail JEDEC retention or speed bins at deep discounts and run them at 4-8x longer refresh; costs ~3% parity and ~50-100 ns added latency, acceptable for a CXL tier, with zero new fab capacity.

title: Automotive remanufacturing: reclaimed server DRAM recertified with defect maps
idea: Adapted from remanufactured auto parts that are torn down, tested and resold with a warranty: retired DDR4/DDR5 RDIMMs from hyperscaler decommissions run through a retention-and-hammer characterization rack built from off-the-shelf FPGA testers, weak rows are written into an SPD-extension defect map, and modules ship with firmware that makes the OS retire those pages at boot.
why: Supply and scarce resources: at ~4x prices, a recertified channel adds bits with zero wafers, helium, quartz or EUV; recovering even 10% of decommissioned modules is a meaningful share of annual bit supply.

title: Outlet-store triage: route reject dies by failure type
idea: Adapted from garment outlets that sort irregulars by flaw type and sell each to a buyer who does not care about that flaw: dies that fail final test are classified on existing testers by signature (retention-weak, speed-weak, hammer-weak, stuck-bit) and packaged into matched products: retention-weak into high-refresh CXL tiers, speed-weak into low-clock edge devices, hammer-weak into read-mostly AI weight stores with low activation rates.
why: Yield and cost per bit (fact 4): each failure type is harmless in some workload; recovering 3-5% of currently scrapped dies adds bits from existing trailing and current lines with no new capacity.

title: Battery cell matching: retention-matched rank assembly
idea: Adapted from EV battery packs, which group cells of matched capacity so one weak cell does not limit the pack: dies are binned by measured retention (e.g., 64/128/256 ms classes) on existing testers, modules are assembled only from same-class dies, and the class is written to SPD so the controller sets tREFI per rank instead of for the worst die in a mixed rank.
why: Refresh cost (fact 3): today one weak die forces worst-case refresh on its whole rank; matched ranks let 60-80% of modules run 2-4x longer refresh, cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss with only assembly-flow changes.

title: Wine-cellar memory: cold-plate DIMM sleds that multiply retention
idea: Adapted from cold-chain storage, where lowering temperature slows spoilage exponentially: memory sleds use existing data-center liquid cold plates to hold DRAM at 35-45 C instead of 70-85 C, and controllers drop to the longer refresh interval valid at low temperature, which also lets leakier, cheaper die bins qualify.
why: Refresh and retention tail (fact 3): leakage roughly halves every ~10 C, so a 30-40 C drop gives ~8-16x retention margin; refresh energy and bandwidth loss can fall up to ~75% and lower-grade dies become usable.

title: Library LOCKSS: peer GPU replicas serve as ECC for weights
idea: Adapted from digital-preservation networks ('Lots Of Copies Keep Stuff Safe') that repair a corrupted copy from peers: in data-parallel inference and training, weights are already replicated on many GPUs, so HBM weight regions run detection-only parity with ECC disabled, and a detected error triggers a 64 B fetch of the same address from a peer GPU's replica over NVLink or Ethernet.
why: HBM capacity and cost (facts 5, 6): reclaims ~12.5% ECC capacity and sideband bandwidth for weight regions and lets lower-grade HBM stacks be used, with firmware and runtime changes only.

title: Video error concealment for KV-cache and activation memory
idea: Adapted from video decoders that conceal lost macroblocks by interpolating from neighbors instead of stopping playback: KV-cache and activation buffers get one parity bit per 32-bit word, and when parity fails the runtime replaces the corrupted element with the mean of the same head's adjacent tokens (or zeroes it and renormalizes attention) instead of raising a machine check.
why: ECC overhead and refresh (facts 3, 8): detect-only parity costs ~3% instead of 12.5% and lets the cache run longer refresh at higher BER; transformers are robust to sparse token corruption, so the largest inference memory consumer moves to cheaper bits.

title: Air-traffic separation zones filled with checkable parity
idea: Adapted from air-traffic control, which keeps separation buffers between aircraft but watches them with radar: the OS page allocator places guard rows between security domains (ZebRAM-style), but instead of leaving them empty fills each with XOR parity of its neighboring data rows; guard rows are verified and rewritten at each scrub, so a hammer flip in a guard is detected and any flip in a data row is correctable.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): guard rows normally waste up to ~50% capacity; storing parity in them turns wasted space into correction capability on existing DRAM with software only.

title: Humbucker twin-cell mode on commodity DRAM for critical data
idea: Adapted from humbucking guitar pickups that pair two opposite-polarity coils to cancel hum: the controller uses the simultaneous multi-row activation already demonstrated on off-the-shelf DDR chips to write a row and its complement into a paired row on the opposite bitline side, so the sense amp sees a differential signal; critical pages (kernel, page tables, keys) run in this twin mode at half capacity.
why: Retention and row hammer (facts 3, 9): differential twin cells give ~2x signal and common-mode disturbance rejection, potentially extending retention 10x+ and resisting hammering for the few percent of memory that needs it, with no new silicon.

title: Catalyst regeneration: in-field thermal anneal heals aged DRAM
idea: Adapted from refineries that regenerate fouled catalyst with heat instead of replacing it: DIMMs carry a thin-film PCB heater and thermistor (board-level and trailing-node parts) and, during scheduled windows with data evacuated, bake their dies at ~150-175 C for about an hour to anneal interface traps and restore hydrogen passivation degraded by hot-carrier and hammer stress.
why: Retention tail and aging (facts 3, 9): trap generation drives variable retention and rising error rates; partial recovery could extend module life and keep refresh rates low, stretching the installed base without new wafers.

title: Telecom regenerator: 65nm DIMM coprocessor for refresh and hammer defense
idea: Adapted from optical-network regenerators that clean signals in-line without the endpoints knowing: a small 65 nm chip beside the register clock driver snoops the command/address bus, keeps approximate per-row activation counts in SRAM, and injects targeted refresh-management commands and retention-aware refresh skipping on the module itself, independent of the host controller.
why: Row hammer and refresh (facts 3, 9): moves mitigation off the leading-edge DRAM die and off the host, so older DRAM dies without in-DRAM counters can serve securely; built entirely in mature logic fabs.

title: Chaos engineering certifies software so memory specs can relax
idea: Adapted from Netflix-style chaos engineering, which injects failures in production until systems tolerate them: a hypervisor-level injector flips random bits in tagged memory regions at controlled rates, and applications that pass sustained injection at BER ~1e-7 are certified to run on relaxed memory pools with weaker ECC, longer refresh and lower-bin dies.
why: Cost per bit and supply: creates demand for lower-reliability bits that existing fabs can produce with relaxed test and repair, raising sellable yield without new capacity.

title: CDN edge caching: weak memory tier holds only clean data
idea: Adapted from CDNs, which can lose a cached object because the origin always has a copy: the OS places only clean, file-backed pages (page cache, read-only model files, container images) on a pool of cheap low-grade DRAM with detection-only codes, and any detected error simply invalidates the page and refetches it from SSD.
why: Cost per bit (facts 3, 4): page cache is often 30-60% of server memory; serving it from salvaged or relaxed-spec DRAM frees premium DRAM for dirty data, and an error costs a ~50 us refetch instead of a crash.

title: Food use-by dates: refresh-free perishable memory for short-lived data
idea: Adapted from perishable-food logistics, which ships milk faster than its shelf life instead of preserving it: a 28 nm logic-compatible 2T/3T gain-cell memory built in existing mature fabs never refreshes; allocations carry an expiry timestamp shorter than the measured retention, and the runtime places only short-lived data (activations, gradient buckets, network buffers) there, reallocating before expiry.
why: Refresh energy and capacity (fact 3): much of the AI working set lives microseconds to milliseconds; serving it from refresh-free trailing-node memory removes refresh cost and offloads leading-edge DRAM.

title: Cybersecurity honeypots: decoy rows tripwire hammering in real time
idea: Adapted from honeypots and canary tokens in network security: the OS seeds each bank with decoy pages holding known patterns physically adjacent to rows owned by untrusted tenants; a high-rate scrubber reads only the decoys, and any flip in a decoy pinpoints the aggressor rows for migration and tenant throttling.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): deterministic detection on existing DRAM without counters, spending ~1% capacity on decoys and focusing scrub bandwidth on <1% of rows.

title: Theatre understudy: on-module spare die shadows the riskiest die
idea: Adapted from theatre understudies who rehearse the lead's part so the show goes on: an RDIMM carries one extra die whose data path is steered by a trailing-node mux; firmware watches per-die correctable-error trends and continuously mirrors whichever die is degrading fastest into the understudy, swapping it out with no data loss when it crosses a threshold.
why: Field failure and screening cost: modules can be built from lower-bin dies because the single most likely failure is pre-mirrored; one spare per 10 dies (~10% capacity) can replace stricter and costlier screening.

title: Airline fare classes: reliability-tiered cloud memory pricing
idea: Adapted from airline fare classes that sell the same seat at different prices with different guarantees: cloud providers offer VM memory in three tiers (full Chipkill ECC, single-error correction on relaxed refresh, detect-only on salvaged DRAM) at stepped prices, backed by separate physical pools and SLA terms stating error rates.
why: Supply and cost per bit: monetizes lower-reliability bits that would otherwise be scrapped and shifts tolerant workloads (batch analytics, caches, inference) off premium DRAM, stretching scarce supply.

title: Aviation dissimilar redundancy: cross-vendor ECC words
idea: Adapted from fly-by-wire systems that use dissimilar processors from different vendors so one design flaw cannot fail every channel: each ECC codeword in a module or CXL pool is assembled from dies of at least three different vendors or process lots, so a vendor-specific weakness (a hammer-sensitive layout, a lot-wide retention excursion) can hit only one symbol.
why: Row hammer and correlated failures (facts 3, 9): chipkill assumes independent dies, but real failures cluster by vendor and lot; dissimilar assembly makes existing ECC far stronger in practice and lets riskier lower-bin parts fill each slot.

title: Telecom line coding: hammer-aware coset scrambling chosen per row
idea: Adapted from line codes (8b/10b, DC-balanced scramblers) that avoid patterns a channel handles badly: the memory controller tries 4 scrambler seeds on each row write and picks the one that minimizes known worst-case victim-aggressor stripe patterns (alternating data opposite to neighbors), storing the 2-bit seed index in spare ECC bits.
why: Row hammer and pattern-dependent retention (facts 3, 9): flip probability depends strongly on data pattern; avoiding worst patterns could raise the effective hammer threshold ~2-5x on existing chips with controller logic only.

title: HPC algorithm-based fault tolerance for AI weight matrices
idea: Adapted from ABFT in scientific computing, where matrices carry row and column checksums so errors are found from the math itself: weights are stored with one checksum row and column per 128x128 tile, verified as a side effect of each matmul (output checksum vs checksum-vector product), and corrected by locating the intersecting failing row and column; DRAM ECC is turned off for those regions.
why: Capacity and bandwidth (facts 5, 6): ~1.5% checksum overhead replaces 12.5% ECC, freeing ~11% HBM capacity and allowing lower-grade stacks, with no hardware change.

title: TLC-NAND strategy: relaxed-window DRAM on idle trailing DRAM lines
idea: Adapted from the NAND industry's move to TLC/QLC, which accepted far worse raw cells because controllers could correct them: older 2x/1x-nm DRAM lines run with loosened process windows (fewer capacitor rework loops, short retention screens, minimal fuse repair) to produce raw-grade dies sold only into ECC-heavy CXL controllers.
why: Capital intensity and supply (fact 4): idle or fully depreciated trailing DRAM capacity becomes productive; relaxed screens and repair raise yield and throughput 10-20% and cut test cost, feeding a cheap controller-corrected tier.

title: CRT degaussing: trap-reset pulses to tame variable-retention cells
idea: Adapted from degaussing coils that reset magnetized CRT masks with a decaying field: using existing vendor test modes on current dies, the controller periodically applies a short decaying-amplitude negative wordline and plate bias sequence to idle subarrays, trying to drive variable-retention traps into their low-leakage state and hold them there.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): variable-retention cells force pessimistic refresh because they toggle unpredictably; if trap states can be biased, the worst-case tail could shrink ~2x, allowing longer refresh on parts already in the field.

title: Vinyl pre-emphasis: controller-boosted restore for flagged weak rows
idea: Adapted from vinyl recording's RIAA pre-emphasis, which boosts fragile high frequencies at cutting time so they survive playback: the controller keeps a small table of rows identified as weak and issues their writes and refreshes with extended tRAS/tWR (or back-to-back double activation) so their cells are fully restored to VARY instead of being truncated by tight default timings.
why: Retention tail (fact 3): many weak cells are under-restored rather than truly leaky; full restore on the ~0.1% flagged rows recovers ~10-20% charge and lets the whole device run a longer refresh interval, in controller firmware on existing chips.
